tasks.routeTitle: Generic linear changes and induction on generators
tasks.currentSketch: For algebraically dependent generators a_i, choose a polynomial relation. Replace variables by generic linear combinations so the relation becomes monic in the last variable (over infinite base field); then that generator is integral over the algebra generated by the others. Induct until remaining generators are algebraically independent.

tasks.entryName: Noether normalization lemma
tasks.entryDescription: Generic linear changes and induction on generators; dimension/transcendence-degree argument; graded algebra/homogeneous forms.
tasks.currentSketch: If A is a finitely generated domain over k, choose maximal algebraically independent subset of its fraction field. Every other generator is algebraic over k(t_1,…,t_d); clear denominators to make A integral over a localization of k[t_i]. The lemma requires a further normalization argument to remove denominators; transcendence degree alone is not enough.

tasks.entryName: Noether normalization lemma
tasks.entryDescription: Generic linear changes and induction on generators; dimension/transcendence-degree argument; graded algebra/homogeneous forms.
tasks.currentSketch: For a graded algebra generated in degree one over infinite k, select a linear form avoiding finitely many components so quotient dimension drops; induction yields algebraically independent homogeneous parameters and A finite over their polynomial subalgebra. This is the graded/homogeneous normalization route.

tasks.entryName: Nullstellensatz
tasks.entryDescription: Maximal ideals and Zariski's lemma; Rabinowitsch trick; algebraic geometry via affine varieties and coordinate rings.
tasks.currentSketch: If I is a proper ideal in k[x_1,…,x_n], choose maximal m⊃I. Zariski's lemma says the field k[x]/m is finite algebraic over k; for algebraically closed k it equals k, so m=(x_i−a_i). Therefore every proper ideal has a common zero (weak Nullstellensatz). The strong form follows by adjoining t and using Rabinowitsch.

tasks.entryName: Nullstellensatz
tasks.entryDescription: Maximal ideals and Zariski's lemma; Rabinowitsch trick; algebraic geometry via affine varieties and coordinate rings.
tasks.currentSketch: If f vanishes on V(I), then in k[x,t] the ideal (I,1−tf) has no zero, hence is the unit ideal by weak Nullstellensatz. Substitute t=1/f in an identity and clear denominators to get f^N∈I.

tasks.entryName: Nullstellensatz
tasks.entryDescription: Maximal ideals and Zariski's lemma; Rabinowitsch trick; algebraic geometry via affine varieties and coordinate rings.
tasks.routeTitle: algebraic geometry via affine varieties and coordinate rings
tasks.currentSketch: An affine variety X has coordinate ring k[X]; maximal ideals correspond to points over algebraically closed k, and radical ideals are intersections of maximal ideals containing them. Thus I(V(I))=√I. This geometric formulation is equivalent to the theorem and uses weak Nullstellensatz.

tasks.entryName: Primitive element theorem (finite separable extensions)
tasks.entryDescription: Inductively choose a linear combination avoiding finitely many bad coefficients; use embeddings into an algebraic closure and count conjugates; finite-field cyclicity as the finite-field special case.
tasks.routeTitle: Inductively choose a linear combination avoiding finitely many bad coefficients
tasks.currentSketch: For separable K(α,β)/K, its distinct K-embeddings give finitely many pairs (σ(α),σ(β)). Choose c∈K avoiding finitely many bad ratios where σ(α+cβ)=τ(α+cβ) for distinct embeddings; then α+cβ has all extension-degree conjugates, so generates. Iterate over generators; K must be infinite.

tasks.entryName: Primitive element theorem (finite separable extensions)
tasks.entryDescription: Inductively choose a linear combination avoiding finitely many bad coefficients; use embeddings into an algebraic closure and count conjugates; finite-field cyclicity as the finite-field special case.
tasks.routeTitle: use embeddings into an algebraic closure and count conjugates
tasks.currentSketch: In a separable closure, embeddings of K(α,β) distinguish conjugate pairs. A generic linear form α+cβ separates all pairs, so has [L:K] distinct conjugates, forcing K(α+cβ)=L. Avoid finitely many c; finite base fields are handled separately by cyclicity of finite-field multiplicative groups.

tasks.entryName: Primitive element theorem (finite separable extensions)
tasks.entryDescription: Inductively choose a linear combination avoiding finitely many bad coefficients; use embeddings into an algebraic closure and count conjugates; finite-field cyclicity as the finite-field special case.
tasks.routeTitle: finite-field cyclicity as the finite-field special case
tasks.currentSketch: A finite subgroup of a field's multiplicative group is cyclic: for each divisor d, roots of X^d−1 are at most d, which forces the group exponent to equal its order; an element of full order exists in a finite abelian group. Thus every finite field extension is generated by a primitive element. This only treats finite fields.

tasks.entryName: Spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators
tasks.entryDescription: Maximize Rayleigh quotient and iterate; compactness yields an eigenvector then orthogonal decomposition; variational min–max principle.
tasks.currentSketch: For compact self-adjoint T, maximize |⟨Tx,x⟩| on the unit sphere using compactness of T(B); variational differentiation gives an eigenvector for an extremal eigenvalue. Its orthogonal complement is invariant; iterate. Nonzero eigenvalues tend to zero and residual space is kernel.

tasks.entryName: Spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators
tasks.entryDescription: Maximize Rayleigh quotient and iterate; compactness yields an eigenvector then orthogonal decomposition; variational min–max principle.
tasks.routeTitle: compactness yields an eigenvector then orthogonal decomposition
tasks.currentSketch: Compactness sends a maximizing sequence for operator norm to a subsequence whose images converge; self-adjointness and variational estimates show the limit direction is an eigenvector with eigenvalue ±||T||. Restrict to its invariant orthogonal complement and repeat; compactness forces eigenvalues→0.

tasks.entryName: Spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators
tasks.entryDescription: Maximize Rayleigh quotient and iterate; compactness yields an eigenvector then orthogonal decomposition; variational min–max principle.
tasks.currentSketch: The Courant–Fischer min–max characterization successively selects extremal Rayleigh quotients on orthogonal complements, producing eigenvectors and ordered eigenvalues; compactness ensures extrema are attained. This is a variational restatement of the iterative proof, requiring compact self-adjoint T.

tasks.entryName: Stone's representation theorem for Boolean algebras
tasks.entryDescription: Ultrafilters/maximal ideals; duality with compact zero-dimensional Hausdorff spaces; prime ideal theorem.
tasks.currentSketch: For Boolean algebra B, let X be ultrafilters, and set U_b={u:b∈u}. These clopen sets satisfy Boolean operations and separate ultrafilters; compactness follows because any cover without finite subcover yields a family with finite intersection property extendable to an ultrafilter. Thus B≅Clop(X).

tasks.entryName: Stone's representation theorem for Boolean algebras
tasks.entryDescription: Ultrafilters/maximal ideals; duality with compact zero-dimensional Hausdorff spaces; prime ideal theorem.
tasks.routeTitle: duality with compact zero-dimensional Hausdorff spaces
tasks.currentSketch: Map each b to U_b in the compact zero-dimensional Hausdorff space X of ultrafilters. Every clopen subset is compact and covered by basic U_b, hence is a finite union and itself U_b; injectivity follows from ultrafilter separation. This constructs the duality directly.

tasks.entryName: Stone's representation theorem for Boolean algebras
tasks.entryDescription: Ultrafilters/maximal ideals; duality with compact zero-dimensional Hausdorff spaces; prime ideal theorem.
tasks.currentSketch: The prime ideal theorem (Boolean prime ideal theorem) extends every proper filter to an ultrafilter. Use these ultrafilters as points; if a family of basic closed sets has finite intersection property, extend the corresponding filter to one point, proving compactness and the representation. This is the choice principle at work, not an independent construction.

tasks.entryName: Nielsen–Schreier theorem (subgroups of free groups are free)
tasks.entryDescription: Schreier rewriting and a transversal; fundamental groups of covering graphs and spanning trees; graph-folding methods.
tasks.currentSketch: Choose a Schreier transversal T for right cosets H\F(X), prefix-closed. For each t∈T and generator x, define s(t,x)=tx(overline{tx})^{-1}∈H. Nontrivial such elements freely generate H: rewrite any word by inserting transversal representatives; uniqueness of reduced words proves no relations.

tasks.entryName: Nielsen–Schreier theorem (subgroups of free groups are free)
tasks.entryDescription: Schreier rewriting and a transversal; fundamental groups of covering graphs and spanning trees; graph-folding methods.
tasks.routeTitle: fundamental groups of covering graphs and spanning trees
tasks.currentSketch: A subgroup H acts freely on the Cayley tree of a free group. The quotient is a graph with π₁ equal to H; choose a spanning tree. Each edge outside it gives one free generator of π₁, so H is free.

tasks.entryName: Nielsen–Schreier theorem (subgroups of free groups are free)
tasks.entryDescription: Schreier rewriting and a transversal; fundamental groups of covering graphs and spanning trees; graph-folding methods.
tasks.currentSketch: Fold a labelled graph representing H until it is immersed in the rose; its core graph has fundamental group H. A spanning tree gives a free basis from non-tree edges. This is the graph-theoretic form of Schreier rewriting; folding is not a distinct underlying principle from covering graph theory.

tasks.entryName: Every finite integral domain is a field
tasks.entryDescription: Multiplication by a nonzero element is injective and hence surjective on a finite set; finite multiplicative group/inverses; polynomial root-counting in a finite domain.
tasks.routeTitle: Multiplication by a nonzero element is injective and hence surjective on a finite set
tasks.currentSketch: For a≠0, multiplication m_a:D→D is injective since D has no zero divisors. On a finite set it is surjective, so 1=ab for some b; every nonzero a is invertible.

tasks.entryName: Every finite integral domain is a field
tasks.entryDescription: Multiplication by a nonzero element is injective and hence surjective on a finite set; finite multiplicative group/inverses; polynomial root-counting in a finite domain.
tasks.currentSketch: The nonzero elements form a finite cancellative multiplicative monoid. For each a≠0, powers repeat, a^i=a^j; cancel a^i to get a^{j−i}=1, hence a has an inverse. This is the finite-semigroup argument equivalent to injective-surjective multiplication.
